newsitem.title: USA: Dollar collapses after hitting 39-month high vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar collapses after hitting 39-month high vs mark.

text.p: The dollar collapsed after surging to a 39-month high against the German mark as dealers booked profits ahead of a European finance ministers' meeting and in reaction to speculation that Europe's single-currency plans could be delayed.

The U.S. currency briefly soared to 1.7423 marks -- its highest level since February 1994 -- after employment reports in the United States and Germany showed the sharply divergent prospects of the two economic powerhouses.
However, the dollar rally soon reversed as speculative traders who had previously bought dollars cashed in their profits.
"European leaders have a meeting on Sunday and people want to square up before this meeting," said Hans Boman, chief spot dealer at Swedbank in New York.
The dollar closed near its session lows, falling to 1.7247 marks from 1.7380 at the open and 1.7290 at Thursday's close. The dollar also slipped to 114.40 yen from 115.72 on Thursday.
Also spurring dollar sales was market talk that a delay would be announced at the Sunday ECOFIN gathering in Europe's plan to launch a single currency, to be called the euro, at the start of 1999.

"The dollar hasn't yet fully played out the increased possibility of a delay. It is vulnerable to retrace some of the gains it saw earlier in the week against the mark," said Bob Lynch, currency strategist at Banque Paribas in New York.

The dollar's slide escalated shortly after the U.S. midday as the rumour of a delay announcement grabbed the market and dragged the dollar below significant technical levels which triggered even more selling.

"The dollar just collapsed. We've broken down very quickly," said James Powers, a vice president in sales and advisory at Westdeutsche Landesbank, minutes before the dollar bottomed out at 114.50 yen and 1.7220 marks.
Dealers found little solace in European officials' insistence that the euro would meet its 1999 launch date.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said Friday that monetary union would go ahead on time, and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reiterated that Germany would meet the budget deficit target required for membership in the single currency and said no talk of an EMU delay had surfaced in Bonn.
Earlier in the day, weak German job data led some to question Germany's ability to meet the strict fiscal criteria.

Figures from the German Bundesbank showed 11.4 percent of Germans were out of work in May, compared with 11.2 percent in April, while the U.S. jobless rate unexpectedly fell to 4.8 percent in May, its lowest level since October 1973.

But a weaker-than-expected U.S. 138,000-job rise in May payrolls, while counteracted by upward revisions to the March and April figures, caused some to question the immediate need for higher interest rates.

"You could talk a bit that the number was neutral for Fed policy, but with stocks and bonds so strong, I don't think you can get a whole lot out of that argument," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. in Chicago.
The British pound partially recovered by the U.S. close from overnight weakness despite a rise of a quarter of a percentage point in British interest rates to 6.5 percent.
The pound closed lower at $1.6320 from $1.6345 at Thursday's close, but above its opening level of $1.6220.
The dollar rose to 1.45 Swiss francs from 1.4455 and to Canadian $1.3832 from C$1.3775.
